deep_dive.title: Multilingual Brain Decoding Reveals Shared Cortical Semantic Geometry
deep_dive.abstract: Human languages differ markedly in lexical and syntactic form yet can convey similar semantic content. The neural basis of this cross-language semantic commonality remains unclear. Here we developed a multilingual brain decoding framework and analysed brain recordings from 227 participants spanning Chinese, English and French. We found that cortical semantic representations exhibited consistent semantic geometry relationships across languages and individuals, revealing a shared cortical semantic geometry. Importantly, the cross-language consistency of cortical semantic geometry increased from sensorimotor to higher-order association cortex, forming a shared semantic geometry gradient closely aligned with the principal cortical functional gradient. Our work establishes generalizable multilingual brain decoding and identifies stable cortical semantic geometry as a neural basis for semantic commonality across languages.

deep_dive.title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
deep_dive.abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.

quick_skim.title: Multiscale Temporal-Spectral-Spatial EEG Learning With Modality-Specific and Modality-Invariant Representations for Emotion Recognition
quick_skim.abstract: Multimodal physiological signals provide complementary cues for emotion recognition. They also raise two related challenges. Emotion-related EEG patterns vary across time, frequency bands, electrodes, and brain regions. Different physiological modalities also contain both modality-specific and shared affective information. This paper presents GMSI-Net, an EEG-centered multimodal emotion recognition framework. It has three key components. The temporal-spatial-spectral-region (TSSR) encoder models multiscale temporal-channel patterns, differential entropy features, and local-to-global brain-region relations. The modality-specific representation (MSR) branch uses bidirectional cross-modal attention and learnable gates. It controls information transfer while retaining modality-specific cues. The modality-invariant representation (MIR) branch learns a shared affective representation. An adaptively weighted contrastive loss aligns this representation across modalities. Independent multiscale Conv-Transformer encoders process the peripheral physiological signals. GMSI-Net is evaluated on DEAP and MAHNOB-HCI using within-subject random ten-fold cross-validation. The model reaches 96.21 (1.47) and 96.41 (1.60) for valence and arousal on DEAP. It reaches 94.10 (2.86) and 94.48 (3.77) on MAHNOB-HCI. These results indicate that combining EEG features with complementary physiological information can improve emotion recognition.

quick_skim.title: Rethinking EEG Spatial Super-Resolution as Dynamic State Decomposition and Filtering
quick_skim.abstract: EEG spatial super-resolution aims to recover high-density neural signals from sparse electrode observations. Existing methods have achieved substantial progress through spatial modeling, generative reconstruction, and temporal representation learning. However, the current EEG state contains two different sources of information: predictable evolution inherited from preceding states and newly emerging changes revealed by the current observation. Most approaches typically do not model these two components explicitly. In this work, we formulate streaming EEG spatial super-resolution as a sequential state filtering problem and propose Dynamic State Filtering (DSF). Rather than relying on a single temporal reconstruction pathway, DSF combines a history-aware dynamical branch with an innovation-filtering branch that explicitly decomposes waveform-state estimation into prediction and observation-driven correction. To infer how spatially incomplete innovations should affect missing locations, DSF routes the observed innovations across electrodes through a mask-constrained, topology-aware transition operator and incorporates them through uncertainty-aware state correction. The two complementary estimates are finally fused to reconstruct the dense EEG signal. Experiments on SEED, SEED-IV and BCI2000 demonstrate that DSF improves reconstruction fidelity and downstream utility while maintaining robustness under dynamically changing and unreliable sparse observations.

quick_skim.title: CNN-based classifier for subject-independent MBTI Extraversion/Introversion preference classification from short-time EEG signals
quick_skim.abstract: This study examines whether short, minimally preprocessed EEG segments contain sufficient information to distinguish between individuals classified as extraverted or introverted according to the Myers--Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI). EEG recordings from 50 participants were divided into 4-s segments and analyzed using a subject-independent nested 5-fold cross-validation procedure to compare EEGNet, EEGProgress, and a newly proposed compact convolutional architecture, SSCNet. SSCNet achieved the highest mean accuracy (0.6481), AUC (0.7063), and F1-score (0.6276). The proposed architecture also showed the lowest variability across folds. SSCNet demonstrated the best computational efficiency, with the shortest median training epoch time and the highest training throughput despite having a similar number of trainable parameters to EEGProgress. The results suggest that MBTI Extraversion--Introversion preferences may be moderately predictable from short time-domain EEG segments without manual spectral feature extraction, while highlighting the importance of subject-independent validation and computationally efficient model design.

quick_skim.title: Observability-Aligned Diffusion and Null-Space Completion for EEG Source Localization
quick_skim.abstract: Electrophysiological source imaging is severely underdetermined because the lead-field matrix has limited rank relative to the source dimension and strongly correlated columns. Scalp EEG measurements constrain only the observable row-space component, leaving a high-dimensional null space unobservable. We propose a two-stage framework coupling posterior diffusion refinement with deterministic null-space completion. A minimum-norm-initialized, singular-coordinate Posterior-DDIM sampler combines a spatiotemporal diffusion prior with direction-dependent measurement reliability to refine the observable component. A frozen ridge predictor and nonlinear temporal residual network then estimate the null component under explicit projection constraints, preserving the refined row estimate and its predicted EEG exactly. All learned components are trained exclusively on simulated cortical activity and its row-null decomposition, without paired EEG-source training data. Across simulations with varying noise levels, the method achieved higher frame-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and average precision, together with lower localization error, than conventional and learning-based baselines. Exploratory evaluations on evoked EEG and simultaneous scalp EEG-stereo-EEG recordings showed condition- and event-dependent concordance with cross-modal and intracranial references.
